claims.claim: Water is one of the six classes of nutrients, and nutrition texts classify it as a macronutrient, a substance the body needs in large amounts; the working definition used in this lesson is that water is the body's essential solvent and transport medium.
Water makes up roughly 50 to 60 percent of an adult's body weight; Harvard's Nutrition Source cites about 60 percent as the adult average, and the share varies with age and body composition.

Water does four headline jobs: it helps manage body temperature (sweating keeps the body from overheating), transports substances through the body in blood, lubricates joints and tissues, and carries waste products away for elimination.

Water comes from two sources, drinks and food; food supplies about 20 percent of total water intake (Harvard), and recommended water intake explicitly includes fluids consumed from both foods and beverages (OpenStax).

Water leaves the body continuously through breath, sweat, and urine; Harvard describes water as restoring fluids lost through metabolism, breathing, sweating, and the removal of waste, and MedlinePlus lists sweating and urinating among the main ways water is lost.
Water carries zero calories, which is why it does not appear in calorie counting yet remains an essential nutrient.

The balance principle: daily water intake (drinks plus food) roughly matches daily water loss (breath, sweat, urine); practical guidance on amounts, thirst, and hydration status belongs to the sibling hydration topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Popular '8 glasses a day' rule versus individualized fluid needs
positions: Common saying: aim for eight glasses of water a day

Harvard's Nutrition Source: this may not be appropriate for every person; the National Academy of Medicine suggests adequate intakes of about 13 cups of daily fluids for men and 9 cups for women, with higher amounts for physical activity and hot climates
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids prescribing amounts. It teaches the general body-weight figure, the two-source split, and the balance principle, and refers all intake targets and hydration guidance to the sibling hydration topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Body-water percentage varies by age and body composition
positions: Harvard: about 60% of an adult's body weight
Common textbook range: roughly 50-60% for adults; infants run higher and older adults lower
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the general range (about 50 to 60 percent of adult body weight) and states that the share varies, without asserting subgroup numbers it did not verify.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated phase-4 draft contained no verifiable water facts: it was generic boilerplate ('Water is a foundational concept in Nutrition...', 'Think of water as a label on a toolbox drawer') with no numeric, mechanistic, or sourced claims, so none of its statements could be verified and all of its wording was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generic draft with a water-specific, source-verified lesson.
Added the working definition (water as the body's essential solvent and transport medium), attributed to the OpenStax nutrition text.
Corrected the draft's implicit framing of water as a course concept; the lesson now teaches water as an actual nutrient with roles, sources, losses, and a balance principle.
Added all quantitative figures (about 50-60% of adult body weight; about 20% of intake from food) with explicit attribution.
rightsIssues: None. All sources were used as reference only. OpenStax content is CC BY 4.0, but no prose was adapted beyond short attributed phrases; MedlinePlus and Harvard pages are cited without reproducing their wording.

sourceRecords.title: 1.1 What Is Nutrition? (Nutrition for Nurses)
sourceRecords.notes: Already registered in the phase-1 source registry; reused with an identical URL. Verified via Wayback Machine capture: classifies water among the macronutrients (needed in large amounts) alongside carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, with vitamins and minerals as micronutrients. Supports water's status as a nutrient in the six-class scheme.

sourceRecords.title: The Nutrition Source: Water
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-22. Supports: water accounts for about 60% of an adult's body weight; about 20% of total water intake comes from water-rich foods such as fruits and vegetables; water restores fluids lost through metabolism, breathing, sweating, and removal of waste, keeps the body from overheating, lubricates joints and tissues; water is calorie-free. Tier B source used alongside Tier A government/open-textbook sources.
